name: Wambule
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 8 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Opgenort, Jean Robert. 2004. A Grammar of Wambule: grammar, lexicon, texts and cultural survey of a Kiranti tribe of eastern Nepal. Brill's Tibetan Studies Library 5/2. Leiden: Brill (Google Books ids 8axxEQAAQBAJ, K8Pb9ylrMRkC; doi:10.1163/9789047414131). Corroborated at open-text grade by Opgenort 2004, 'A technique for writing Wambule', Libju-Bhumju 24 (author's site, the Internet Archive 2016-03-16) and Opgenort 2010, 'On adopting the Limbu script for Wambule', Libju-Bhumju 41 (the Internet Archive 2013-11-27); second-hand by the Sampang word-accent chapter in Bielmeier & Haller (eds.) 2007, Linguistics of the Himalayas and Beyond, Mouton de Gruyter (Google Books id FO2l6ptuKt4C, excerpt).
catalog_locator: Opgenort 2004, ch. 2 'Phonology', sec. 2.1.1 'Phonemic length', p. 56 (the stress statement: first three sentences of the section) and p. 60 (negated verbs: 'The word stress generally falls on the root following the negative prefix', with examples [e'sitsem] etc.); ch. 3 'Morphophonology', sec. 3.2.1 'Lexical affixes', p. 101 (negative prefix <a> 'does not function as the stressed open syllable of a polysyllabic verb'; 'The negative marker is the only prefix in Wambule'). Pages are the Google Books page anchors (pg=PA56, PA60, PA101), identical in both volumes 8axxEQAAQBAJ and K8Pb9ylrMRkC; p. 55 carries the running head 'CHAPTER TWO — PHONOLOGY', p. 101 the running head 'MORPHOPHONOLOGY'. The same passage in the 2002 dissertation is pp. 59-60 (cited as 'Opgenort 2002: 60' in the Sampang chapter and '2002: 59-60' in Borchers 2008). Open-text corroboration (Opgenort 2004a, 'A technique for writing Wambule'): section 'Phonological analysis'.
catalog_quote: [ch. 2, sec. 2.1.1 Phonemic length, p. 56] In Wambule, word stress or relative prominence of a syllable due to an increase of loudness usually falls on the root of verbs and deverbatives and on the initial syllable of nouns and other parts of speech . Word stress is indicated in phonetic transcription if it does not fall on the initial syllable of the phonological word, especially in negated verbs . The stressed open syllable of polysyllabic words is characterised by a distinctive length contrast between the phonemes / i / and / i: /, / a / and / a: /, and / u / and / u: / . ... [ch. 2, p. 60] ... stressed open syllable of polysyllabic words are also present in the stressed open syllable of polysyllabic verbs that are marked with the negative prefix <a> . The word stress generally falls on the root following the negative prefix . / AsicAm / [ e'sitsem] ' to not die, not be dead ' / Asi: cAm / [ e'si: tsem] ' to not thread, not bind ' ... [ch. 3, sec. 3.2.1 Lexical affixes, p. 101] ... The negative prefix is analysed as a lexical prefix which occurs in each negated form . This marker does not function as the stressed open syllable of a polysyllabic verb . ... The negative marker is the only prefix in Wambule . ... [Opgenort 2004a, 'A technique for writing Wambule', open text:] In Wambule, vowel length is distinctive in the initial open syllable of polysyllabic words except negated verb forms. Vowel length is generally lost or neutralised in the remaining phonological environments. ... The contrast between /ya/ and /e/ and between /wa/ and /o/ is phonologically relevant in initial stressed syllables: /syacAm/ स्याचाम syacam ‘to pluck’ /secAm/ सेचाम secam ‘to be swept’ /swacAm/ स्वाचाम swacam ‘to say, talk’ /socAm/ सोचाम socam ‘to tell’

Vowel length is generally lost or neutralised in the remaining phonological environments. [...] The contrast between /ya/ and /e/ and between /wa/ and /o/ is phonologically relevant in initial stressed syllables: /syacAm/ स्याचाम syacam 'to pluck' /secAm/ सेचाम secam 'to be swept' /swacAm/ स्वाचाम swacam 'to say, talk' /socAm/ सोचाम socam 'to tell' The contrast between postconsonantal /ya/ and /e/ and between /wa/ and /o/ is only marginally distinctive in other syllable types.

Only differences: the report uses straight quotes where the file has curly o…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No explicit stress rule is stated in any source opened. Opgenort's own texts equate the syllable that carries full vowel contrasts (length, /ya/~/e/, /wa/~/o/) with 'the initial open syllable of polysyllabic words' (2004a, 2002 summary) and with 'the stressed open syllable of polysyllabic words' (2010), and speak of 'initial stressed syllables' in disyllabic infinitives; taken together these imply that word stress in polysyllabic words falls on the first syllable, with non-initial syllables reduced (neutralised vowel quality/length, archiphonemes A, I, U). This is an inference from the describer's wording, not a quoted placement rule; the explicit statement will be in Ch. 2 of the 2004 grammar (not accessible).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Negated verb forms are excluded from the initial-syllable length contrast ('except negated verb forms'); 'some closed monosyllabic verb forms' keep a length contrast (2010). Nothing on loanwords or on stress in compounds.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (polysyllabic words, cited in phonemic transcription; examples are verb infinitives in -cAm). Unclear whether stress is phonemic; the language is presented as non-tonal (no tone is listed among the phonemes in either article).
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Wambule of Hilepānī village (Okhalḍhuṅgā district), Opgenort's main field site; Opgenort treats Wambule and Jero (jero1239) as two mutually intelligible dialect groups of one 'Chaurasia' language, and the ASJP/CLDF and older sources use the names 'Chouras'ya', 'Chourase', 'Umbule'. Glottolog wamb1257 = Wambule [wme].
